title: The Siege Begins and the Prophet's Wife Dies
summary: On the day Nebuchadnezzar lays siege to Jerusalem, God tells Ezekiel to write down the date and gives him a parable of a rusted cooking pot set on the fire, a picture of the bloodstained city that cannot be cleansed. Then Ezekiel's wife, the delight of his eyes, dies suddenly, and he is forbidden to mourn in public. His silence becomes a sign: when the temple, the delight of Israel's eyes, is destroyed, the people will be too stunned to mourn.
story: This chapter is the hinge of Ezekiel. For twenty-three chapters he has warned that Jerusalem would fall; now the siege has begun, and the long argument is over. The book turns after this to oracles against the nations (chapters 25 to 32), and it returns to Israel in chapter 33, where a survivor arrives in Babylon with news that the city has fallen (33:21-22). Chapter 24 also ties off a thread from the beginning of the book. Since his call, Ezekiel has been largely silent except when God gave him a word (3:26-27). Verse 27 promises that on the day the news arrives, his mouth will be opened. The prophet's private grief and the nation's public catastrophe are bound together in a single sign.
historical:
The date in verse 1, the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year, is the same date given in 2 Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4 for the start of Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem. On the usual reckoning it falls in January 588 BC, though some scholars, using a different calendar starting point, place it a year later. The siege lasted a year and a half or more, depending on which chronology is followed, and ended with the city's capture in the summer of 587 or 586 BC. The date was remembered: after the exile, the prophet Zechariah mentions a fast of the tenth month (Zechariah 8:19), and Jewish tradition still keeps a fast on the tenth of Tevet in memory of the siege.

Ezekiel was hundreds of miles away in Babylonia, and the chapter presents him as knowing on the day itself what was happening at Jerusalem. That is why he is told to write down the date: when news later came, the written record would show that the word had come from God.
cultural:
The cooking pot recalls a saying of Jerusalem's leaders quoted in 11:3: the city is the pot, and we are the meat, meaning they were the choice portions, safe inside the walls. God takes up their image and turns it against them. The pot will boil, its contents will be emptied without anyone casting lots over the pieces, and the pot itself will be heated empty until its corrosion burns away. The law required that the blood of a slaughtered animal be poured on the ground and covered with dust (Leviticus 17:13). Blood left on bare rock was blood unacknowledged and unatoned, crying out like Abel's (Genesis 4:10).

The mourning customs that Ezekiel is forbidden to keep were well known. Mourners removed their headdress and sandals, covered the lower part of the face or the lips (compare Leviticus 13:45; Micah 3:7), wailed publicly, and ate food brought by neighbors, the bread of mourners (Jeremiah 16:7; Hosea 9:4). Not to mourn a wife would have looked unthinkable, which is exactly why the people ask what it means.
literary: The chapter has two parts joined by the theme of loss. Verses 1 to 14 are a parable in the form of a work song, possibly adapted from a song sung while cooking: put the pot on, pour in water, add the best pieces. After the song, two woe oracles (verses 6 to 8 and 9 to 14) interpret it and twist it into judgment. Verses 15 to 27 are a sign-act, the last and most personal in the book. The key phrase is the desire of your eyes, used first of Ezekiel's wife (verse 16) and then of the temple (verses 21 and 25). The narrative is terse: I spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening my wife died. The restraint of the telling matches the restraint of the prophet.

outline.t: Write down the date: the siege has begun
Woe to the city of bloodshed: the rusted pot
The pot heated empty: judgment without pity
The meaning: the temple lost, grief beyond mourning
The fugitive's news and the prophet's opened mouth

doctrines.note: The rusted pot shows a judgment that comes after cleansing was offered and refused (verse 13). God is not rushing to judge; he has tried to purify, and the city would not be purified.
The chapter lets a prophet's personal loss become part of his message. Ezekiel's grief is real, and the text does not explain it away; it shows him obeying while carrying it.
Ezekiel knows the siege has begun on the day it happens and records the date so that the word can be tested. The book presents prophecy as God's word that proves true in history.

words.note: Machmad, desire or delight, something precious that the eyes rest on with love. It is used of Ezekiel's wife and of the temple, drawing a line between a man's dearest person and a nation's dearest place. The word makes the loss personal on both sides.
Chel'ah, rust or corrosion, found as a common noun only in this passage of the Old Testament. It stands for defilement so deep in the city that even fire struggles to burn it away.
Sir, a pot or cauldron used for cooking, including cooking sacrificial meat. The city's leaders once boasted that Jerusalem was a pot protecting them; here the pot becomes the place of judgment.

christ: Ezekiel's life becomes a sign to his people (verse 24): he bears in his own household the grief that is coming to the nation. That pattern, a prophet whose body and life carry God's message, reaches its fullest form in Jesus, who not only spoke about the fall of Jerusalem but wept over it (Luke 19:41-44) and warned of the temple's destruction (Mark 13:1-2). Jesus also spoke of his own body as the temple, destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19-21). Where Ezekiel's grief pointed to the loss of the house where God dwelt, Christ's death and resurrection are presented in the New Testament as the making of a new dwelling place of God. These are connections of pattern drawn by later writers; Ezekiel's own horizon is the fall of the city in his day.

hard.q: Did God really take Ezekiel's wife to make a point, and why forbid him to grieve?
hard.a: The text is stark. God tells Ezekiel he will take the desire of his eyes, and that evening she dies. Readers rightly flinch. Some interpreters read God's words as foreknowledge rather than cause: God tells his prophet that his wife will die and directs how that death, already approaching, will become a sign. Others accept that the text presents the death as God's act and place it within the Bible's wider confession that life and death are in God's hands, without claiming to explain why this woman died when she did. On the command not to mourn, it is important to see what is forbidden. Ezekiel is told to groan quietly (verse 17). He is not told to feel nothing; he is told not to perform the public rituals of mourning, so that his silence would become a sign of the numb, stunned grief of people whose loss is too great for ritual. Many readers find the passage one of the most human in the book, because it shows the cost a prophet paid. It should not be read as a general teaching that believers must suppress grief; elsewhere Scripture gives grief full voice, in the psalms of lament, in Lamentations, and in Jesus weeping at the grave of Lazarus (John 11:35).

questions: Ezekiel was told to write down the date so that the word could be checked. Why does it matter that biblical prophecy makes claims that can be tested in history?
The pot was offered cleansing and would not be purified. What makes a person or community resist being made clean?
Ezekiel's private grief became part of his public witness. How have your own losses shaped what you have to say to others?
